## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]). **Inference:** an ability
with a long residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, 30 ± 5 d) can be built early and
carried further without direct work than a short-residual one, but a stage longer than about
30 days after accumulation ends needs a retention dose (see Example); max speed (5 ± 3 d)
needs re-exposure close to competition. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.

**When NOT to apply** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

# Realization Mesocycle: One to Three Weeks, Much Lower Load, Built Around Maximal Speed and Rehearsed Competition Behavior

**What it is** — The realization mesocycle is "traditionally... termed the taper" (PDF p. 122,
printed p. 111; verified against page image). In traditional periodization the taper precedes
important competitions (the book does not itself say "only"); under Block Periodization it is
broader, forming the
concluding phase of **every** training stage (see
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]), so a season contains several
realization mesocycles of differing weight depending on the upcoming competition's importance.
Athletes enter this mesocycle fatigued from the preceding transmutation mesocycle, so the first
objective is restoration toward supercompensation by competition day; the targeted abilities
(maximal speed/quickness, event-specific tactics, competition readiness) all require high CNS
reactivity, available energy resources, and mental concentration, states only available to a
well-rested athlete, which is why workload reduction is described as "of paramount importance"
at the mesocycle's start. Table 3.12 (PDF p. 123, printed p. 112; verified against page image)
gives the full prescription: **aims**, peak-performance attainment, full restoration before
competition, and completing the training stage's overall program (peaking demands scale with
the competition's level/importance); **targeted abilities**, maximal speed/quickness,
event-specific tactics, readiness to compete; **workload level**, "much lower than in
preceding mesocycles," with various approaches to how that reduction is achieved (the
"valid" qualifier is the writer's, not the book's);
**duration**, **one to three weeks**, depending on competition importance and sport-specific
factors; **techno-tactical improvement**, via sport-specific modeled exercises/tasks that must
build genuine competitive performance (the "not just rehearsal" framing is the writer's own
gloss on this requirement, not the book's wording); **emotional tension/anxiety**,
elevates as competition approaches, more so for higher-stakes competition; **monitoring**,
follow-up time-trials, techno-tactical execution quality, training responses, and restoration
level, focused on integrative sport-specific estimates and each athlete's most important
individual traits; **nutrition**, deliberate use of supplements and energy-intake control to
produce an ergogenic effect and prevent unwanted body-composition change. On workload-reduction
timing: a **short** mesocycle demands a fast decrease; a **longer** one allows gradual
reduction; duration itself is "extremely important and sensitive" because a too-long taper
risks detraining while a too-short one may not restore and develop event-specific abilities
adequately (a contradiction Issurin attributes to Mujika et al., 2004). Techno-tactical
simulation must (1) reproduce the competitive situation as closely as possible, (2) approximate
competitive concentration levels, and (3) repeat enough to build stable, reliable skill. Issurin also gives the taper's own mood evidence, separate from the anxiety discussion below:
"workload reduction during the taper causes a remarkable improvement in mood associated mainly
with improved recovery" (citing a review by Mujika et al., 2004, PDF p. 124, printed p. 113).
Table
3.13 (PDF p. 124, printed p. 113) gives a worked dosage for a **two-week realization mesocycle
for qualified kayakers**: quasi-competitive race performance, 4-6 total; race simulation in
broken series (four quarters, 20s breaks), 8-12; selective simulation of the initial race
quarter, 10-16; selective simulation of the two mid-race quarters, 8-12; simulation of the
pre-event warm-up program, 3-5. On emotional tension: pre-competition anxiety can cut either
way, moderate anxiety facilitates performance, excessive anxiety detracts from it, and elite
athletes are reported to benefit more from increased anxiety than sub-elite athletes, while
mid-class athletes can be "sharpened" by emotional tension (Raglin & Wilson, 2000, stated this
way in the source; the sub-elite/mid-class distinction is not further clarified there). Table
3.14 (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114) gives realization-specific monitoring indicators: sprint-
repetition and simulation totals; maximal-speed and event-simulation test results; effort
perception; HR and blood lactate after relevant exercises; CPK and urea; resting HR; sleep
quality and mood questionnaire; body mass and fat component. Issurin also states four benefits
of keeping the monitoring program consistent across successive realization mesocycles within a
season (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114): coaches can validate the test set against real
competitive outcomes over time; individual (not just group) norms can be established for each
athlete; athletes themselves learn to read their own responses; and self-regulation and
body-mass management methods can be set in advance rather than improvised. Issurin adds a
specific nutrition warning, illustrated by a case
study: **20 highly qualified male long-distance triathletes**, tracked across a 4-week
high-workload mesocycle into a **2-week taper mesocycle** (PDF pp. 126-127, printed pp.
115-116, based on Margaritis et al., 2003): average energy intake stayed roughly
flat. The text states energy expenditure "decreased... by up to 69.3%" during the taper (PDF
p. 126, printed p. 115); Figure 3.10 (PDF p. 127, printed p. 116; re-verified against the page
image, 2026-09-27) instead plots reduced-workload expenditure at about **69% of** the
high-workload level, i.e. roughly a 31% fall, not a 69% one (the chart's own axis, 50-110%,
could not plot a fall to about 31% of baseline). This is a source inconsistency, not a
transcription error on this entry's part; the figure reading is the more plausible one given
the axis range, and both are recorded here rather than silently harmonized. Mean body mass
didn't change, but body fat mass **increased by 4.3%** (about 104.3% of baseline, matching the
figure). Issurin's point: unchanged body mass can mask
a real fat gain (or muscle loss) if eating habits don't adjust downward with the drop in
training energy cost, so body mass alone is "not always a reliable" anthropometric indicator
during a taper. **Inference, from the primary abstract (Margaritis et al., 2003, *Journal of
the American College of Nutrition* 22:147-156):** this was a double-blind antioxidant-
supplementation trial with a supplemented group (n = 7) and a placebo group (n = 9), 16
athletes analyzed, not 20 as the book states; the abstract does not report the energy-balance
or body-composition figures the book cites, so those specific numbers could not be verified
against the primary source and should be treated as the book's own retelling.

**Why it works** — The core mechanism is the same reduced-load-toward-supercompensation logic
already given for the pre-competitive microcycle
(see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]], which is this mesocycle's dominant
microcycle type): the targeted abilities need a well-rested nervous system and available energy
stores, so load must come down before those specific qualities can actually be trained and
expressed. The duration-sensitivity point (too long detrains, too short under-restores) is
Issurin's own applied synthesis, though he cites Mujika et al. (2004), a real, checkable
taper-physiology review, as the source flagging this contradiction in the field generally,
not something Issurin resolves with his own data here.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep** is the
clearest college-football analog to a full one-to-three-week realization mesocycle: workload
should come down substantially from whatever preceded it (regular-season maintenance load, or a
short rebuild block if the last-game-to-bowl gap was used as a mini accumulation/transmutation
sequence, see [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]), practice time
should shift toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavily rehearsed, opponent-specific

143	# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities
144	
145	**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
146	induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
147	training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
148	printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
149	printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
150	motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
151	**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
152	**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
153	lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
154	muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
155	maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
156	enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
157	printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
158	enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
159	1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
160	phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
161	(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
162	p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
163	quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
164	kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.
165	
166	**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
167	aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
168	"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
169	sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
170	are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
171	are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
172	organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
173	morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
174	area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
175	activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
176	endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
177	anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
178	residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.
179	
180	**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
181	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]). **Inference:** an ability
182	with a long residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, 30 ± 5 d) can be built early and
183	carried further without direct work than a short-residual one, but a stage longer than about
184	30 days after accumulation ends needs a retention dose (see Example); max speed (5 ± 3 d)
185	needs re-exposure close to competition. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
186	residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
187	re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
188	readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
189	programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
190	pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
191	week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
192	"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
193	~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.
194	
195	**When NOT to apply** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
196	(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
197	per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
198	(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
199	source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
200	thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
201	weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
202	1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
203	aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).
204	
205	**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
206	states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
207	lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
208	(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
209	This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
210	30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
211	not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
212	capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
213	windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
214	p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
215	ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
216	the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
217	decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
218	marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
219	with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
220	loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
221	not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
222	`contested`, with this as the stated reason.
223	
224	**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
225	Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
226	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
227	staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
228	gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
229	heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
230	as restating the same specific claim.
231	
232	**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
233	(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
234	realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
235	aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
236	this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
237	an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
238	needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
239	have decayed well below peak by competition day.
240	
241	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
242	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
243	fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
244	cross-reference, do not conflate),
245	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
246	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

260	
261	# Realization Mesocycle: One to Three Weeks, Much Lower Load, Built Around Maximal Speed and Rehearsed Competition Behavior
262	
263	**What it is** — The realization mesocycle is "traditionally... termed the taper" (PDF p. 122,
264	printed p. 111; verified against page image). In traditional periodization the taper precedes
265	important competitions (the book does not itself say "only"); under Block Periodization it is
266	broader, forming the
267	concluding phase of **every** training stage (see
268	[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]), so a season contains several
269	realization mesocycles of differing weight depending on the upcoming competition's importance.
270	Athletes enter this mesocycle fatigued from the preceding transmutation mesocycle, so the first
271	objective is restoration toward supercompensation by competition day; the targeted abilities
272	(maximal speed/quickness, event-specific tactics, competition readiness) all require high CNS
273	reactivity, available energy resources, and mental concentration, states only available to a
274	well-rested athlete, which is why workload reduction is described as "of paramount importance"
275	at the mesocycle's start. Table 3.12 (PDF p. 123, printed p. 112; verified against page image)
276	gives the full prescription: **aims**, peak-performance attainment, full restoration before
277	competition, and completing the training stage's overall program (peaking demands scale with
278	the competition's level/importance); **targeted abilities**, maximal speed/quickness,
279	event-specific tactics, readiness to compete; **workload level**, "much lower than in
280	preceding mesocycles," with various approaches to how that reduction is achieved (the
281	"valid" qualifier is the writer's, not the book's);
282	**duration**, **one to three weeks**, depending on competition importance and sport-specific
283	factors; **techno-tactical improvement**, via sport-specific modeled exercises/tasks that must
284	build genuine competitive performance (the "not just rehearsal" framing is the writer's own
285	gloss on this requirement, not the book's wording); **emotional tension/anxiety**,
286	elevates as competition approaches, more so for higher-stakes competition; **monitoring**,
287	follow-up time-trials, techno-tactical execution quality, training responses, and restoration
288	level, focused on integrative sport-specific estimates and each athlete's most important
289	individual traits; **nutrition**, deliberate use of supplements and energy-intake control to
290	produce an ergogenic effect and prevent unwanted body-composition change. On workload-reduction
291	timing: a **short** mesocycle demands a fast decrease; a **longer** one allows gradual
292	reduction; duration itself is "extremely important and sensitive" because a too-long taper
293	risks detraining while a too-short one may not restore and develop event-specific abilities
294	adequately (a contradiction Issurin attributes to Mujika et al., 2004). Techno-tactical
295	simulation must (1) reproduce the competitive situation as closely as possible, (2) approximate
296	competitive concentration levels, and (3) repeat enough to build stable, reliable skill. Issurin also gives the taper's own mood evidence, separate from the anxiety discussion below:
297	"workload reduction during the taper causes a remarkable improvement in mood associated mainly
298	with improved recovery" (citing a review by Mujika et al., 2004, PDF p. 124, printed p. 113).
299	Table
300	3.13 (PDF p. 124, printed p. 113) gives a worked dosage for a **two-week realization mesocycle
301	for qualified kayakers**: quasi-competitive race performance, 4-6 total; race simulation in
302	broken series (four quarters, 20s breaks), 8-12; selective simulation of the initial race
303	quarter, 10-16; selective simulation of the two mid-race quarters, 8-12; simulation of the
304	pre-event warm-up program, 3-5. On emotional tension: pre-competition anxiety can cut either
305	way, moderate anxiety facilitates performance, excessive anxiety detracts from it, and elite
306	athletes are reported to benefit more from increased anxiety than sub-elite athletes, while
307	mid-class athletes can be "sharpened" by emotional tension (Raglin & Wilson, 2000, stated this
308	way in the source; the sub-elite/mid-class distinction is not further clarified there). Table
309	3.14 (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114) gives realization-specific monitoring indicators: sprint-
310	repetition and simulation totals; maximal-speed and event-simulation test results; effort
311	perception; HR and blood lactate after relevant exercises; CPK and urea; resting HR; sleep
312	quality and mood questionnaire; body mass and fat component. Issurin also states four benefits
313	of keeping the monitoring program consistent across successive realization mesocycles within a
314	season (PDF p. 125, printed p. 114): coaches can validate the test set against real
315	competitive outcomes over time; individual (not just group) norms can be established for each
316	athlete; athletes themselves learn to read their own responses; and self-regulation and
317	body-mass management methods can be set in advance rather than improvised. Issurin adds a
318	specific nutrition warning, illustrated by a case
319	study: **20 highly qualified male long-distance triathletes**, tracked across a 4-week
320	high-workload mesocycle into a **2-week taper mesocycle** (PDF pp. 126-127, printed pp.
321	115-116, based on Margaritis et al., 2003): average energy intake stayed roughly
322	flat. The text states energy expenditure "decreased... by up to 69.3%" during the taper (PDF
323	p. 126, printed p. 115); Figure 3.10 (PDF p. 127, printed p. 116; re-verified against the page
324	image, 2026-09-27) instead plots reduced-workload expenditure at about **69% of** the
325	high-workload level, i.e. roughly a 31% fall, not a 69% one (the chart's own axis, 50-110%,
326	could not plot a fall to about 31% of baseline). This is a source inconsistency, not a
327	transcription error on this entry's part; the figure reading is the more plausible one given
328	the axis range, and both are recorded here rather than silently harmonized. Mean body mass
329	didn't change, but body fat mass **increased by 4.3%** (about 104.3% of baseline, matching the
330	figure). Issurin's point: unchanged body mass can mask
331	a real fat gain (or muscle loss) if eating habits don't adjust downward with the drop in
332	training energy cost, so body mass alone is "not always a reliable" anthropometric indicator
333	during a taper. **Inference, from the primary abstract (Margaritis et al., 2003, *Journal of
334	the American College of Nutrition* 22:147-156):** this was a double-blind antioxidant-
335	supplementation trial with a supplemented group (n = 7) and a placebo group (n = 9), 16
336	athletes analyzed, not 20 as the book states; the abstract does not report the energy-balance
337	or body-composition figures the book cites, so those specific numbers could not be verified
338	against the primary source and should be treated as the book's own retelling.
339	
340	**Why it works** — The core mechanism is the same reduced-load-toward-supercompensation logic
341	already given for the pre-competitive microcycle
342	(see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]], which is this mesocycle's dominant
343	microcycle type): the targeted abilities need a well-rested nervous system and available energy
344	stores, so load must come down before those specific qualities can actually be trained and
345	expressed. The duration-sensitivity point (too long detrains, too short under-restores) is
346	Issurin's own applied synthesis, though he cites Mujika et al. (2004), a real, checkable
347	taper-physiology review, as the source flagging this contradiction in the field generally,
348	not something Issurin resolves with his own data here.
349	
350	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep** is the
351	clearest college-football analog to a full one-to-three-week realization mesocycle: workload
352	should come down substantially from whatever preceded it (regular-season maintenance load, or a
353	short rebuild block if the last-game-to-bowl gap was used as a mini accumulation/transmutation
354	sequence, see [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]), practice time
355	should shift toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavily rehearsed, opponent-specific
356	game-plan simulation (the Table 3.13 dosage pattern, adapted from race-quarters to game-plan
357	segments, e.g., specific down-and-distance packages, specific special-teams looks), and staff
358	should watch emotional tension deliberately given a long layoff and a non-conference,
359	lower-frequency opponent-preparation rhythm. **The gap between the final regular-season/
360	conference-championship game and the bowl game** is exactly the scheduling problem Issurin's
361	duration-sensitivity warning describes: too long a "taper-only" approach across that whole gap
362	risks detraining (per Mujika et al., 2004, and consistent with
363	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]'s ~30-day residual windows for
364	basic abilities), which is the direct rationale for treating the early part of that gap as a
365	short accumulation/transmutation rebuild and only the final 1-3 weeks before the bowl as this
366	realization mesocycle. The nutrition warning (unchanged eating during a lower-workload window
367	risks fat gain even at stable body mass) is directly transferable to any football taper or bowl
368	prep window and worth flagging to Performance Nutrition specifically, since body-composition
369	oversight sits with that separate Health & Wellness unit per Eric's baseline
370	(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition"). **Eric's baseline** gives no duration
371	band or nutrition-adjustment guidance for a taper window anywhere in `method-baseline.md`; the
372	closest material is the general in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume," citing
373	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21, which is compatible in direction but supplies
374	none of this entry's specificity (the one-to-three-week band, the competition-importance
375	scaling, or the body-composition-during-taper warning).
376	
377	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** every piece of
378	supporting data here
379	(the kayaker simulation dosage, the triathlete nutrition case) comes from individual endurance
380	sports with single, clearly-defined competitive efforts; football has no equivalent single
381	"race" to simulate, and a "game" cannot be rehearsed at full competitive intensity the way a
382	kayak race segment can. The triathlete case (per the primary abstract) is n=16 (7+9), one study,
383	one sport, with no reported statistical test of the 4.3% fat-mass change's significance in this
384	text: treat the direction (unadjusted eating during a taper risks fat gain) as a plausible,
385	citable caution, not a precise, guaranteed effect size for a football population with very
386	different body-composition targets and energy demands than a long-distance triathlete. The 1-3
387	week duration band and the anxiety-by-athlete-level claim (Raglin & Wilson, 2000) are stated
388	without further detail on that study's own population or method in this text. This mesocycle's
389	emotional-tension guidance assumes a single identifiable peak competition; it does not address
390	a multi-game bowl-adjacent context (e.g., a conference championship immediately followed by a
391	short turnaround into a bowl selection process) where emotional tension may need to be managed
392	across two closely spaced high-stakes events rather than one clean taper. **Inference, from the
393	staging Verkhoshansky fitness-fatigue entry:** Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991) found "presently
394	accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results"
395	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]],
396	staging). This sits in tension with Issurin's own position that a short realization mesocycle
397	"demands a fast workload decrease" (PDF p. 123, printed p. 112): Fitz-Clarke's caution and
398	Issurin's fast-decrease prescription for short tapers point in opposite directions on how
399	aggressive a short taper's load cut should be, and this text does not resolve that tension.
400	
401	**Example** — **Inference:** a three-week bowl-prep plan could open with a lighter first week (still
402	carrying some team-practice volume, closer to a short transmutation-mesocycle tail) that
403	tapers hard into a genuine one-to-two-week realization phase immediately before the game,

405	football, energy intake reviewed alongside the drop in practice volume, and staff watching for
406	either excess complacency (too little anxiety, given the layoff and often lower-stakes framing
407	of some bowl games) or excess anxiety in players for whom the bowl carries personal stakes
408	(e.g., a senior's final game, an NFL draft evaluation window).

434	# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly
435	
436	**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
437	names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
438	where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
439	(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
440	maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
441	decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
442	effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
443	injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
444	Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
445	specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
446	determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
447	109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001," a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
448	splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
449	targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
450	Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
451	then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts** (Tuesday and Wednesday
452	mornings, maximal strength plus explosive strength as the secondary modality), combined with a
453	medium-load team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout
454	(Wednesday afternoon). This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the Wednesday
455	strength key-workout before mini-block 2's team-practice key-workout begins, to let the
456	anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
457	**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
458	preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (Thursday
459	afternoon, itself the microcycle's **third key-workout**, "substantial or big" load, intended
460	to deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session
461	immediately before the game itself (Saturday, mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the
462	specific forthcoming opponent). Figure 3.8 shows a total of three key-workouts across the
463	week, not two. Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
464	Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
465	extra preparation; he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
466	chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
467	which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
468	cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
469	ballistic explosive-type microcycles to enhance jump performance instead.
470	
471	**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated reason (PDF p. 111, printed p. 100): weekly
472	competition stress "restrict[s] the benefits of utilizing BP mesocycle sequencing. However,
473	the benefits of accentuating dominant training targets, in a mini-block structure, and
474	designing key-workouts can be attained." **Inference:** this is the chapter's direct answer to
475	the constraint stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs
476	concentrated, sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend
477	competition long enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
478	(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
479	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
480	normally require in duration); splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
481	each with its own key-workouts, is a way of keeping some of BPC's concentration benefit even
482	though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several, but the author frames it
483	as attaining benefits under a restriction, not as a full substitute for mesocycle sequencing.
484	
485	**When to apply: this is the entry most directly answering the in-season half of the
486	strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
487	(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
488	is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
489	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
490	pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
491	early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
492	while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
493	the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. **Inference:** the
494	28-30 hour recovery window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block
495	gives a specific, citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its
496	heaviest in-season lift and the next high-intensity team session; Issurin does not himself
497	generalize this figure beyond the Figure 3.8 worked example.
498	
499	**When NOT to apply** — The specific day-by-day chart (Figure 3.8) is built from
500	one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'
501	in-season concurrent training: a real, checkable citation, but a single study in rugby league,
502	a sport with a different weekly game/practice rhythm than college football, which layers
503	additional constraints (NCAA-mandated practice-time limits, travel, and a Saturday-only game
504	schedule rather than rugby league's varying weekly structure). **Population caveat:** none of
505	this section's evidence comes from American football itself; Issurin lists
506	football alongside soccer, rugby, and volleyball as sports the *problem* applies to, but the
507	worked example and its supporting citation are rugby-specific. **Inference:** the specific
508	"two key-workouts, 28-30 hours recovery" prescription should be treated as a structural
509	template to adapt to football's own practice-count and padded/unpadded-practice rules, not a
510	ready-made in-season lift schedule. Issurin gives no guidance here for bye weeks, short
511	(Thursday-game) weeks, or the postseason gap before a bowl game; those fall outside this
512	weekly-cycle framework and are closer to the pre-competitive/realization material in
513	[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and
514	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]].
515	
516	**Example** — **Inference, following Figure 3.8's actual pattern (PDF p. 109, printed p. 98)
517	for a Sunday game:** Monday AM active recovery/conditioning; Tuesday AM maximal-strength
518	key-workout (plus explosive strength), Tuesday PM medium-load team practice; Wednesday AM
519	second maximal-strength key-workout (plus explosive strength, bigger load), Wednesday PM
520	active-recovery/conditioning; Thursday PM key team practice (substantial-to-big load); Friday
521	off; Saturday AM team practice/technical work (medium load); game Sunday. For a Saturday-game
522	week, this pattern would need to shift roughly one day earlier across the board (e.g., the two
523	strength key-workouts moving to Sunday-Monday and the key team practice to Wednesday), since
524	Issurin's own worked example assumes a Sunday game and does not itself address the shift.
525

545	# When a Training Stage Outruns the 30-Day Residual Clock, Insert a Mini-Block, Don't Just Add Workouts
546	
547	**What it is** — This section directly answers the mismatch already flagged in
548	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]: the accumulation
549	mesocycle's basic-ability residual runs out at about **30 days** (Table 1.6; see
550	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), which caps how long the
551	following transmutation-plus-realization stretch can run before basic abilities decay below
552	target. But Issurin notes many sports need their transmutation mesocycle to run **3-4 weeks**
553	for anaerobic glycolytic development, and the realization mesocycle (taper) can run **about two
554	weeks**: together, roughly **five weeks**, which already exceeds the ~30-day strength-aerobic
555	residual (PDF pp. 129-130, printed pp. 118-119; verified against page image). Issurin's stated
556	fix: do **not** simply add extra aerobic or strength workouts into the transmutation mesocycle
557	to "top up" the decaying residual. This fails because the highly intense transmutation
558	mesocycle actively suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training, and the anabolic
559	strength stimulus needs recovery time the transmutation mesocycle cannot spare. Instead, insert
560	a **special compact mini-block (a short microcycle)** dedicated to the decaying ability. Figure
561	3.12 (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119; re-verified against the page image, 2026-09-27) diagrams the
562	resulting pattern for a training stage, in sequence: **accumulation** (high-volume basic
563	aerobic-strength workloads, **20-25 days**), then **transmutation** (highly intensive specific
564	workloads, **20-25 days**), then **realization** (taper and maximal speed, **10-16 days**), then
565	**competition**. The figure's "Mini-block inclusion" callout points to more than one insertion,
566	not a single one: an accumulation-type (aerobic-strength) patch sits inside the transmutation
567	span, a transmutation-type (highly intensive specific) patch sits inside the realization span,
568	and a second accumulation-type patch also sits inside the realization span: three mini-block
569	insertions total across the diagram, not one. Issurin gives a worked contrast of two
570	real scheduling situations (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120): when two targeted competitions are set
571	**a five-week interval** apart (his cited example: kayaking's European and World Championships,
572	which happen to fall five to six weeks apart in a typical calendar),
573	the fix is to compress the whole stage (10-14 days accumulation, 10-14 days transmutation, 8-10
574	days realization), short enough that the accumulation mesocycle's own residual still covers the
575	whole stage, so **no mini-block is needed at all**. When circumstances instead force a longer,
576	**7-9 week** training stage (his example: pre-Olympic preparation, where the international
577	calendar has no tune-up competitions before the Games), the recommended answer is to plan longer
578	mesocycles **and** include the mini-block, because a stage that long cannot otherwise carry the
579	accumulation-phase residual all the way to competition. **Inference:** the chapter's own summary
580	restates the placement rule concretely: an **aerobic mini-block can be inserted inside the
581	transmutation mesocycle**, and a **highly intense anaerobic mini-block can be inserted inside
582	the realization mesocycle** (PDF p. 132, printed p. 121); reading this alongside Figure 3.12's
583	three patches, each mesocycle gets a short dose of whichever ability it does not otherwise
584	train, timed to arrive before that ability's own residual clock runs out (this synthesis
585	across the figure and the summary sentence is the writer's own connection, not stated by
586	Issurin in one place).
587	
588	**Why it works** — The author gives a reason why *added workouts* fail, but hedges the
589	proposed remedy rather than explaining why it succeeds. His stated reason additional workouts
590	fail, scoped to the transmutation mesocycle specifically: the transmutation mesocycle
591	"strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training," and added strength work
592	"require[s] sufficient recovery that cannot be provided" inside a mesocycle built for a
593	different, fatiguing purpose (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119). For the remedy itself, Issurin
594	writes only: "**Apparently**, what should be inserted in the mesocycle is not several
595	additional workouts but a special compact mini-block (short microcycle), in order to prolong
596	training residuals" (PDF p. 130, printed p. 119), his own hedge word, not a stated mechanism
597	for why a discrete mini-block succeeds where added workouts fail. No outcome data for the
598	mini-block approach is presented in this section; Figure 3.12 cites Issurin & Lustig (2004), a
599	coaching-practice article in *Leistungssport*, not a controlled study. **Inference:** a
600	plausible reason a discrete mini-block might succeed is that it is short enough to insert
601	without abandoning the surrounding mesocycle's main purpose while still being its own coherent
602	loading-then-recovery unit rather than scattered single sessions, but this is the writer's own
603	extrapolation, not something Issurin states.
604	
605	**When to apply: this is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
606	miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap (logged 2026-09-03), and the
607	clearest football calendar mapping in this chapter, Inference throughout** —
608	
609	- **The gap between the final regular-season or conference-championship game and a bowl game**
610	  (commonly roughly 3-6 weeks depending on bowl selection and game date) is structurally the
611	  same scheduling decision Issurin poses in his worked example. A **short** gap (roughly
612	  5-6 weeks or less) should be handled like his compressed-stage case: run a short
613	  accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence sized to fit inside the gap (e.g., 10-14 days
614	  rebuild / 10-14 days sharpen / remaining days as realization/taper), in which case a
615	  strength-aerobic residual built at the very start plausibly survives to the bowl game without
616	  needing a mini-block. A **longer** gap (closer to 6+ weeks, which happens for some
617	  earlier-selected bowls) more closely resembles his 7-9 week pre-Olympic case: plan a longer
618	  rebuild phase **and** insert an aerobic (or strength) mini-block partway through the
619	  bowl-prep transmutation-equivalent work, specifically to protect the basic conditioning base
620	  built early in the gap from decaying below target by game day.
621	- **In-season, week to week:** [[case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]]
622	  already shows that a hard game can itself accelerate residual decay; a bye week, or a week
623	  after an unusually taxing game, is a natural, calendar-given opportunity to run something like
624	  Issurin's aerobic mini-block (a few days of concentrated aerobic-strength work) to "top up" a
625	  basic-ability residual before it drops further, rather than treating every week's training
626	  content as identical regardless of how the prior weeks' games affected the athletes.
627	- **Eric's baseline** does not currently name a mini-block concept or an explicit bowl-prep
628	  periodization structure at all. **Inference:** this is the writer's own assessment, not
629	  Eric's: among the Chapter 3 entries produced so far, this framework reads as the single most
630	  direct, numerically specific answer this ingest has produced to that gap, and should be
631	  flagged to Eric as a candidate structure to react to, not an already-adopted practice.
632	
633	**When NOT to apply** — **Population caveat, repeated deliberately because this is
634	the chapter's central prescriptive claim:** every piece of evidence behind this framework
635	(the 30-day residual table, the kayaking/pre-Olympic worked examples, the Popov case) comes from
636	individual, endurance-or-technical Olympic sports with a fixed, known international competition
637	calendar set months or years in advance. Football's bowl-selection process is itself uncertain
638	until late in the season (a team does not always know its exact bowl date and opponent far in
639	advance), which makes pre-planning an exact-length rebuild-then-taper sequence harder than in
640	Issurin's kayaking example, where the championship dates are fixed well ahead of the season.
641	**Inference:** none of Issurin's specific day-counts (20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16 days; the 5-6 week
642	vs. 7-9 week contrast) were derived from or tested against a team-contact-sport calendar; they
643	should be treated as a structural template to adapt to football's specific bowl-selection
644	timeline and roster fatigue state at season's end (which is itself compounded by an already-long
645	season, unlike Issurin's examples where the "prior mesocycle" is a dedicated, undisturbed
646	accumulation block rather than 12+ weeks of in-season competition). The mini-block's own
647	duration is not specified numerically in this section (Issurin calls it a "short microcycle,"
648	consistent with the 2-4 day aerobic contrast mini-block already given in
649	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]'s Table 3.10):
650	treat 2-4 days as the applicable figure by cross-reference, not as independently stated here.
651	Issurin gives his own explicit limit on this whole residual-clock logic, immediately before
652	this section: "if the training design is based solely on the length of training residuals, it
653	will be extremely rigid and inflexible. There are also other factors influencing training
654	residuals" (PDF p. 127, printed p. 116); the training stage itself he defines as three
655	consecutive mesocycle-blocks "vary[ing] from 4-10 weeks" (same locator). This entry's
656	day-count-driven Example below should be read against that caveat, not as a rigid formula.
657	Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states that block-periodization evidence "does not
658	supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football"
659	(Issurin, 2016, *Sports Medicine*, vault
660	`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a.md`).
661	
662	**Example** — **Inference:** for a **4-week gap** between a team's last game and its bowl game,
663	Issurin's own worked 5-week case (10-14 / 10-14 / 8-10 days) states plainly that "you need not
664	include mini-blocks because the training residuals following the accumulation mesocycle
665	surpass the competition" (PDF p. 131, printed p. 120); a 4-week gap is shorter still, so by
666	the same logic a plan could run roughly 10 / 10 / 8 days (accumulation / transmutation /
667	realization) with **no mini-block needed at all**, following Issurin's compressed-stage case
668	rather than requiring one. For a **6-week gap**, closer to but still short of Issurin's 7-9
669	week pre-Olympic case, a plan following this framework could run roughly 14-16 / 14-16 / 10-12
670	days **with** an aerobic mini-block inserted partway through the transmutation-equivalent
671	phase, since a stage approaching that length is closer to where Issurin says the accumulation
672	residual alone cannot cover the whole stage; note that Figure 3.12's own 20-25 / 20-25 / 10-16
673	day figures apply to the longer 7-9 week stage, not to a 6-week gap, so they should not be used
674	as the target durations here. Per the caveat above, treat both of these as a structural
675	template to react to, not a rigid formula: "there are also other factors influencing training

699	
700	# Competition Cut Popov's Aerobic-Mesocycle Gains Roughly in Half (V-AT) Within About Ten Days
701	
702	**What it is** — Issurin addresses whether competitions inside a training stage (not the
703	final target competition) help or hurt (PDF pp. 128-129, printed pp. 117-118). His position:
704	mid- and low-level competitions inside accumulation or transmutation mesocycles add useful
705	emotional diversity and elicit training responses that enrich adaptation, but highly intense
706	competitive efforts also trigger a stress-hormone response. The supporting case: Alexander
707	Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World swimming champion) preparation was tracked with an
708	incremental stepwise swimming test measuring anaerobic threshold speed, V-AT (blood lactate =
709	4 mM) and V-La8, the speed producing 8 mM lactate (the stated lower limit of highly intense
710	glycolytic work). Measurements were taken at the start of a highly concentrated aerobic
711	mesocycle, again 10 days later, and again a few days after Popov competed several times
712	(Figure 3.11, PDF p. 129, printed p. 118; re-verified against the page image, 2026-09-27,
713	adapted from Pyne & Touretski, 1993). Both velocity markers rose over the mesocycle's first
714	~10 days (V-AT 1.57 to 1.63 m/s; V-La8 1.64 to 1.72 m/s), then fell after the competition
715	(V-AT to 1.60 m/s at day ~21; V-La8 to 1.70 m/s), a decline the book itself calls "a
716	substantial decrease" (its own wording, not "erased" or "fatigued"). About half of the V-AT
717	gain and about a quarter of the V-La8 gain were lost; both markers remain above their starting
718	values. Issurin attributes this decline to shortened training residuals "induced by the
719	previous program" (PDF p. 128, printed p. 117), i.e. to the competition's effect on the
720	residual clock, not to any stated change in the training content itself.
721	
722	**Why it works — the author's own attributed mechanism, not independently re-derived here** —
723	The book gives two separate chains, not one merged chain (PDF p. 128, printed p. 117): (a)
724	stress hormones (catecholamines, cortisol) reinforce the catabolic process (Viru & Viru, 2001),
725	so "muscle mass and maximum strength can decrease"; and (b), cited to a different source,
726	"the highly intense anaerobic glycolitic efforts typical in competition suppress the activity
727	of aerobic enzymes and the oxidative process in the mitochondria" (Volkov, 1986). The book's
728	conclusion 3 (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118) ties the shortened residual to stress hormones in
729	general; Volkov is specifically the citation behind the glycolytic-suppression chain (b), not
730	the hormonal chain (a). **Inference:** chain (b) is the same physiological substrate underlying
731	aerobic endurance's normal ~30-day residual
732	(see [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]), so a hard competition can
733	be read as an accelerant on that decay clock rather than a separate, independent event; the
734	book does not state this link explicitly. Issurin also notes the field's practical response:
735	"prominent coaches" have "added special aerobic workloads to restore and revitalize the
736	athletes after competition" (PDF p. 128, printed p. 117), a plain author statement, not this
737	entry's own inference.
738	
739	**When to apply** — **Inference:** as a citable, named-athlete illustration for why a program including
740	in-season or in-training-stage competitive tests should expect some real cost to basic-ability
741	residuals, not treat competing as a free additional training stimulus. Directly supports the
742	caution already logged for the transmutation mesocycle
743	(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) about why
744	"including competition" is listed as an *option*, with tradeoffs, rather than an unqualified
745	recommendation. **Inference:** for football, this is a reason to expect that a physically
746	brutal, high-intensity early-season or mid-season game can measurably eat into whatever aerobic
747	or strength base was built in the preceding weeks, not just add acute fatigue that resolves in
748	a few days, which argues for the mini-block "topping up" logic in
749	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] being applied proactively after
750	unusually hard, high-intensity games, not only on a fixed calendar schedule.
751	
752	**When NOT to apply** — This is a single elite swimmer's data, reported secondhand
753	(Pyne & Touretski, 1993, published via Issurin & Lustig, 2004), with no comparison athlete who
754	trained the same mesocycle without competing, and no statistical test of the pre/post-competition
755	change reported in this text: the chart (Figure 3.11) shows one athlete's trajectory, not a
756	group result. **Inference:** swimming's anaerobic-threshold/lactate-based test protocol has no
757	direct football analog; football has no simple single-modality repeated field test that isolates
758	"aerobic threshold" the way a stepwise swim test does, so this exact monitoring approach cannot
759	be copied, only the underlying caution (hard competition costs some residual) can be carried
760	over. This case does not address whether the effect is dose-dependent on competition intensity,
761	duration, or the athlete's fitness level entering the competition.
762	
763	**Example** — **Inference:** a strength staff noting that a physically demanding, high-effort game (e.g., a
764	triple-overtime contest, or a game following an unusually taxing travel/short-week schedule)
765	likely cost the team some of the conditioning base built the prior weeks has a named precedent
766	(Popov's threshold-speed decline) for treating that as a real, not just anecdotal, training-load
767	event worth a deliberate light aerobic "top-up" in the following week, rather than assuming a
768	normal recovery day fully addresses it.
769	
770	**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
771	[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
772	[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]],
773	[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]].
