=== strength-and-conditioning/elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept.md
conf: untested | ch: "U1 L5" | Evans's Own Caveat: the Fitness-Fatigue Model Is "Just a Concept," Not an Empirically Validated Model
WHAT:  — Evans's slide (U1 L5 p.3-4) introduces the Fitness-Fatigue Model ("Fatigue can mask fitness") and then immediately qualifies it: "Theoretical Model, only useful if you provide evidence. Marathon running... 400m runner? Strength, speed, jumping, aerobic capacity, etc... No empirical evidence to put a model together with all the biomotor qualities together. JUST A CONCEPT" (capitalization as on the slide). He does not cite a specific paper making this critique; it reads as his own assessment, offered in his own lecturing voice. 
NOT:  — Evans's own caveat is itself unsupported by a named citation ("no empirical evidence" is asserted, not referenced to a specific review or meta-analysis), so it should be read as his professional judgment, not a sourced literature claim. Do not use this entry as evidence that the fitness-fatigue model is definitively unsupported in the broader literature; it records only that Evans, in this lecture, said it lacks empirical evidence for multi-quality application. Confidence is untested. 

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md
conf: contested | ch: "1.16" | "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique
WHAT:  — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than "supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88). The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former [i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized. The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov, 1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed 88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.) 
NOT:  — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact (structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact on periodization design. 

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing.md
conf: supported | ch: "1.16" | The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition
WHAT:  — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant (Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991) found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results, and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.) 
NOT:  — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2) must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that fitting process. Inference: the cited taper studies are 1990s endurance-sport studies (Shepley et al. 1992, middle-distance runners; Zarkadas et al. 1995, triathletes; Mujika et al. 1996, swimmers; the text itself does not name the sports studied); don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to football or other team sports without independent verification. 

=== strength-and-conditioning/periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio.md
conf: supported | ch: "1" | The 3:1 Fatigue-to-Fitness Ratio
WHAT:  — Zatsiorsky and Kraemer (cited by Bompa) propose that the fatigue from a training bout dissipates roughly **three times faster** than the positive training effect persists — e.g., fatigue lasts ~24 hr while the fitness benefit lasts ~72 hr. The positive effect only becomes *visible* once the masking fatigue has cleared; adaptation and improved performance surface afterward. 
NOT:  — The 3:1 figure is a rule of thumb, not a constant. Training type shifts it — anaerobic work is more fatiguing and lengthens the ratio; CNS-intensive work can extend fatigue well past 24 hr. Don't use it to schedule to the hour. Pairs with [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--three-training-effects]]. 

=== strength-and-conditioning/periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle.md
conf: supported | ch: "1" | The Supercompensation Cycle
WHAT:  — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).

=== strength-and-conditioning/elite-sports-performance--evans/heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps.md
conf: untested | ch: "U4 L1" | "Monitoring Is a Compass, Not a GPS Unit"
WHAT:  — Evans's closing slide (U4 L1 p.23, "closing thoughts") states (no attribution shown): "Monitoring is a compass, not a GPS unit. Only utilize it if you believe in the literature and will utilize it to make adjustments to the training process. Start simple and small, but be very consistent. Sometimes the cheaper options provide better insight. Don't get offended if the data is showing your training plan is not working as well as you think it should. LEARNING MOMENT!" 
NOT:  — This is a general philosophy statement, not a specific decision rule; it does not say which specific metrics function well as "compass"-type directional signals versus which might mislead. === strength-and-conditioning/elite-sports-performance--evans/principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time.md
conf: untested | ch: "U3 L4" | Periodization's Central Concept Is Variation and Timing, Not Time Itself
WHAT:  — Evans states (U3 L4 p.16): "Central concept of periodization: VARIATION. Planning and programming to achieve an increase in athletic preparedness and to optimize readiness. The sequence and timing of the application of the training stimulus. It is when you do what you do. Example: Max strength may be important in the preparation, but in the wrong place, it can have negative interactions." A following slide (p.19) restates this as: "The interaction & interdependence of the training components. No training component is in isolation. Timing NOT time." And (p.20): "To have the team or individual ready to perform at their optimum at the appointed time." 
NOT:  — This is a stated planning philosophy, not a specific sequencing rule; the slide does not say which training components interact negatively with which others, or by how much, so it cannot be applied as a checklist without the more specific compatibility material Eric's baseline documents (which itself, per that baseline's own tension log, is Infe

=== strength-and-conditioning/elite-sports-performance--evans/principle--recovery-is-a-training-means.md
conf: untested | ch: "U3 L1" | "Recovery Is Not Simply a Thing. It Is a Part of a Logically Sequenced Training Plan. Recovery Is a Training Means."
WHAT:  — The slide states (U3 L1 p.6, no attribution shown beyond the slide's own text): "Recovery is not simply a 'thing'. It is [sic, slide reads "apart of"] a part of a logically sequenced training plan. Recovery is a training means." This follows a slide on "Preparedness" (p.5) stating: "The best way to increase an athlete's preparedness is to induce restoration and adaptation by implementing a properly designed periodized training program that uses logical variations in volume, intensity, and exercise selection. By including appropriate variation in the training regime, the athlete will have periods of reduced training volume, reduced training intensity, and complete rest, all of which dissipate fatigue, induce adaptations, and increase the athlete's preparedness to perform at a high level.
NOT:  — This is a stated principle, not a quantified prescription; the slide gives no specific formula for how much volume or intensity reduction constitutes adequate "recovery as a training means" for a given athlete or training phase. Confidence is untested.

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence.md
conf: supported | ch: "1.16" | Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops
WHAT:  — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically, these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/ glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed 
NOT:  — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988) without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact three-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than a specific testing checkli

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response.md
conf: supported | ch: "3.5.7" | Ligaments and Tendons Thicken and Strengthen With Training, Weaken With Inactivity
WHAT:  — The authors report that physical training strengthens the attachments of tendons and ligaments to bone: trained ligaments are thicker and heavier, though the increase in mass is not necessarily associated with a greater concentration of collagen, a process described as still poorly understood (Booth & Gould, 1975); controlled strain on soft tissue may increase fibre formation, contributing to enhanced elasticity and strength (Holland, 1968). Regular resistance training increases not only muscle hypertrophy but also the collagen content of ligaments and the connective tissue surrounding muscle fibres (Tipton et al., 1975); training also increases the activity of an enzyme involved in collagen synthesis, an effect possibly stimulated by lactic acid production during exercise (Booth & Gould, 1975). By contrast, moderate-intensity treadmill training in rats produces neither muscle hypertrophy nor increased intramuscular connective tissue growth; prolonged low-intensity training conditions the cardiovascular system but not the musculoskeletal system. "Apparently" it is anaerobic, muscl
NOT:  — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** Much of the underlying evidence is animal-model research (rat treadmill studies; Tipton's ligament work), not human athlete data, and the collagen-concentration-vs-mass distinction is itself described in the source as poorly understood. Do not assume a single stretching or sprint session meaningfully strengthens ligament-bone junctions; the text is explicit this requires chronic training. 

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness.md
conf: supported | ch: "1.5" | Work Capacity, Fitness, and Preparedness Are Three Different Things
WHAT:  — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable: it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue. "Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state, sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44, printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.) 
NOT:  — **Inference:** the terminology mismatch matters: do not assume "preparedness" means the same thing in both sources without checking which sense is meant, since Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the department's "readiness," not its "preparedness." This entry's own definitions above use Verkhoshansky's terms throughout. 

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms.md
conf: supported | ch: "1.1" | Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue
WHAT:  — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into **central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor neuron recruitment and firing rate, a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue** (failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins). Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at >50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15). Two distinct purposes are given for reduced central drive during fatigue, on different pages: for short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in motor-neuron firing rate "may be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and facilitating maximal mechanical response" (printed 15); separately, "muscle wisdom," the CNS's down-regul
NOT:  — **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy, not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so 

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing.md
conf: supported | ch: "3.4.2" | Post-Tetanic Potentiation (the Book's "After-Effect"): Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules
WHAT:  — When a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its subsequent activity is measurably altered, a phenomenon that, "in physiology," is called post-tetanic potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters**: preliminary isometric tension followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase despite fatigue), but with the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric), "results deteriorate" (printed 164). The after-effect "occurs immediately after preliminary isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still retains some trace of inhibitory influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared with its initial level" (printed 164). **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest post-isometric dynamic-strength boost (90%, as printed; this sits beside 6.7% and 5.8% for the other two loads tested and is a probable misprint, though recorded here as given) came after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7% boost
NOT:  — All quantified figures here come from single, older Russian studies (Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961; Klimonov 1965) on specific lifts (barbell squat, isometric leg extension) and specific populations; the load-to-timing relationship is shown as non-monotonic in at least one dataset (25% 1RM peaking fastest, 50% slowest), so this should not be flattened into a single simple "heavier load = later peak" rule. This framework should be read alongside [[cla

=== strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates.md

**What it is** — Natera sketches two team-sport annual plans (~80:44–88:49) and stresses that they are **not plug-in programs**.

**Plan A: eccentric-led.**
- **Offseason:** about 80% of the strength stimulus is eccentric and 10–20% isometric. It opens with long time-under-tension eccentrics at 80–100% RM and longer-duration holds that build toward their load.
- **Then:** ISO pushes enter as grind training at 3–5 s, and the eccentrics move to 4–6 s above 1RM.
- **Around December–January:** supramaximal eccentrics at **110–140%**, 2–4 s. Pushes shift from grind toward explode, and switches and then catches come in.
- **In season:** mostly isometric, with minimal eccentric exposure.

**Plan B: "passive" eccentric emphasis,** for high-volume team sport. It runs low-level isotonic work, then eccentrics from high-volume/light to lower-volume/heavier. Holds follow from about Oct/Nov for roughly two months, switches from mid-January, and catches from mid-March to April. **Volume stays flat and load and exercise intensity carry the progression.**

In both plans, **plyometrics continue throughout**. They are graded on a five-level arbitrary intensity scale, with emphasis splits such as 70/30 and 60/40 between high and low levels. *(Month names reflect his calendar, likely a Southern-hemisphere or Qatar season; all numbers are single-source ASR from slides. Verify at ~81:35–88:02.)*

**Why it works** — The mechanism is **asserted**. "A failed isometric muscle action is essentially an eccentric action," so heavy eccentric work prepares the athlete for high-force isometrics. Late in the year, **holds and quasi-isometrics can stand in for eccentric work**: switches and catches involve some lengthening, and holds (in his claim) share eccentric neural pathways. He reports that eccentric adaptations "stay around" when switches and catches are kept in. That is an observation, not a measured result.

**When to apply** — Fit the structure to the college football year:
- **Winter and early spring:** eccentric-heavy, holds introduced.
- **Summer:** pushes and switches.
- **Fall camp and season:** mostly isometric (pushes, holds, some switches), with short, low-soreness sessions that coexist with game-week running loads.

For staff who are uneasy about heavy eccentrics in season, this gives a rationale for replacing them with holds. **Force-plate hook:** track single-leg iso push peak force and a drop-jump RSI across the season to see whether in-season isometrics actually preserve offseason gains.

**When NOT to apply** — The whole structure is **untested**. It is one coach's template with no comparison group, and the "holds replace eccentrics" and "adaptations stay around" claims are the least supported parts. Supramaximal eccentrics at 110–140% are a real soreness and strain risk in contact-sport camps, so they need a staff with the equipment and experience. The month-by-month placement belongs to his season and needs remapping. It does **not** cover hamstring-specific eccentric work (Nordics); do not read "in season mostly isometric" as permission to drop hamstring eccentrics. For that, see the hamstring-monitoring evidence in [[wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]].

**What it is** — Natera sketches two team-sport annual plans (~80:44–88:49) and stresses that they are **not plug-in programs**.

**Plan A: eccentric-led.**
- **Offseason:** about 80% of the strength stimulus is eccentric and 10–20% isometric. It opens with long time-under-tension eccentrics at 80–100% RM and longer-duration holds that build toward their load.
- **Then:** ISO pushes enter as grind training at 3–5 s, and the eccentrics move to 4–6 s above 1RM.
- **Around December–January:** supramaximal eccentrics at **110–140%**, 2–4 s. Pushes shift from grind toward explode, and switches and then catches come in.
- **In season:** mostly isometric, with minimal eccentric exposure.

**Plan B: "passive" eccentric emphasis,** for high-volume team sport. It runs low-level isotonic work, then eccentrics from high-volume/light to lower-volume/heavier. Holds follow from about Oct/Nov for roughly two months, switches from mid-January, and catches from mid-March to April. **Volume stays flat and load and exercise intensity carry the progression.**

In both plans, **plyometrics continue throughout**. They are graded on a five-level arbitrary intensity scale, with emphasis splits such as 70/30 and 60/40 between high and low levels. *(Month names reflect his calendar, likely a Southern-hemisphere or Qatar season; all numbers are single-source ASR from slides. Verify at ~81:35–88:02.)*

**Why it works** — The mechanism is **asserted**. "A failed isometric muscle action is essentially an eccentric action," so heavy eccentric work prepares the athlete for high-force isometrics. Late in the year, **holds and quasi-isometrics can stand in for eccentric work**: switches and catches involve some lengthening, and holds (in his claim) share eccentric neural pathways. He reports that eccentric adaptations "stay around" when switches and catches are kept in. That is an observation, not a measured result.

**When to apply** — Fit the structure to the college football year:
- **Winter and early spring:** eccentric-heavy, holds introduced.
- **Summer:** pushes and switches.
- **Fall camp and season:** mostly isometric (pushes, holds, some switches), with short, low-soreness sessions that coexist with game-week running loads.

For staff who are uneasy about heavy eccentrics in season, this gives a rationale for replacing them with holds. **Force-plate hook:** track single-leg iso push peak force and a drop-jump RSI across the season to see whether in-season isometrics actually preserve offseason gains.

**When NOT to apply** — The whole structure is **untested**. It is one coach's template with no comparison group, and the "holds replace eccentrics" and "adaptations stay around" claims are the least supported parts. Supramaximal eccentrics at 110–140% are a real soreness and strain risk in contact-sport camps, so they need a staff with the equipment and experience. The month-by-month placement belongs to his season and needs remapping. It does **not** cover hamstring-specific eccentric work (Nordics); do not read "in season mostly isometric" as permission to drop hamstring eccentrics. For that, see the hamstring-monitoring evidence in [[wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]].

Lewis 2021 — Athlete monitoring in American collegiate football
POP:  - Thirty-five Virginia Tech football athletes aged 18–24 contributed to the broader monitoring dataset across seven position groups; all were medically cleared and consented. [p. 58] - The two CMJ studies each used five highly trained collegiate football athletes, so their estimates are exploratory

[pp. 91–94] - In the acute-fatigue study, jump height, relative mean power, and peak velocity showed moderate immediate reductions that were small by 24 hours, whereas flight-time-to-contraction-time ratio and reactive strength index modified showed large reductions that remained large at 24 hours. [pp. 96–97] - Eccentric and concentric durations increased immediately after training and remained elevated 24 hours later, suggesting that athletes could preserve some output by changing movement strategy. [p. 97] 
LIM:  - The dissertation explicitly identifies observational and associational designs, purposive non-probability sampling, lack of researcher control over training exposure, and dependence on maximal effort during jump testing; causal inference is not supported. Lever et al. 2026 — Game exposure, per-snap intensity, and performance in Division I football
POP:  - Longitudinal observational data comprised 4,084 player-games from 232 athletes, 88 games, and 10 seasons within one NCAA Division I football program. [p. 5] - Players were grouped as Bigs, Mids, Skills, or quarterbacks and by game exposure: low (0–22 snaps), moderate (23–49), or high (≥50). [p. 4
KEY:  - Total external load increased across exposure groups, but per-snap load decreased. Per-snap PlayerLoad was 8.73 AU·snap−1 lower for moderate versus low exposure (95% CI 7.71–9.76; d=0.83) and 11.60 AU·snap−1 lower for high versus low exposure (95% CI 10.50–12.70; d=1.10). [p. 6] - Exposure-related reductions in per-snap load occurred across positional groups, although absolute and per-snap loads varied by position and metric. [p. 6] - On offense, total PlayerLoad (β=0.015, p<0.001), sprinting distance (β=0.0108, p=0.001), and impact count (β=0.106, p<0.001) were positively associated with PFF grade. [p. 7] - On defense, total-load associations were limited, while higher per-snap running, sprinting, acceleration, and deceleration metrics were associated with lower PFF grades (all p<0.01). [p. 7] - These load–grade relationships are phase-specific associations and do not demonstrate that accumulating load improves offense or that higher intensity causes worse defense. [p. 10] 
LIM:  - A single Division I program across changing seasons, schemes, coaches, player roles, injuries, and technology limits external validity. [p. 10] - PFF grades are analyst-derived, role- and opportunity-dependent proxies rather than independently validated objective outcomes; small grade differences

Thorpe et al. 2017 — Monitoring fatigue status in elite team-sport athletes
POP:  - This is a narrative brief review of team-sport fatigue monitoring, supplemented with evidence from other sports where team-sport evidence was unavailable. [p. 1] - Much of the applied evidence discussed comes from elite association football, Australian football, rugby, and endurance sport; it is 
KEY:  - Athlete self-report measures appeared responsive to acute and chronic load in several team-sport studies, but the authors state that further work is needed to establish relationships with injury and illness. [p. 2] - Submaximal exercise heart rate, HRV, and heart-rate recovery showed inconsistent or context-dependent responses; the direction of heart-rate changes should not be interpreted as fatigue in isolation. # Updated Review of the Applied Physiology of American College Football: Physical Demands, Strength and Conditioning, Nutrition, and Injury Characteristics of America’s Favorite Game
## Why it may matter
May provide an integrative reference on American college football demands, strength and conditioning, nutrition, and injury characteristics. Full text is unavailable, so this is a retrieval lead rather than reviewed evidence.
## Full-text status
=== research-papers\west-2021-more-than-a-metric-how-training-load-is-used-in-elite-sport-for-athlete-management
West et al. 2021 — Training load as contextual decision support
POP:  - This is a peer-reviewed editorial informed by the authors’ experience across multiple team and individual sports, not an empirical study with participants or measured outcomes. [p. 1] - Examples include association football, American football, basketball, rugby, baseball, and other sports, so pro
KEY:  - **Editorial proposition, not an empirical finding:** tools are valuable when they provide sufficiently accurate information for a defined performance decision while minimizing athlete and practitioner burden. [p. 2] - External and internal load should be interpreted within a model connecting data to a desired outcome; validity, reliability, and utility require evaluation in the intended environment. [p. 2] - The authors explicitly reject any single metric or metric collection as a definitive injury-prediction tool and describe causal links between load and injury as unresolved. [p. 3] - Load data may support five levels of use: feedback, in-session adjustment, day-to-day planning, season planning, and long-term athlete management. [p. 3] - Individual athlete, match, travel, environmental, psychological, career-stage, and organizational context can change interpretation; communication and interdepartmental collaboration are therefore part of the monitoring process. [p. 4] - Monitoring systems should surface critical cues, filter irrelevant data, support staff work, and track progre
LIM:  - The paper is an expert editorial; it does not demonstrate that its framework improves performance, reduces injury, or outperforms alternative decision processes. - Selected examples and citations cannot establish prevalence, causal effects, or universal best practice. - Assertions that rest may r

KEY:  - **Conceptual proposition, not an empirical finding:** distinguish periodic assessment from repeated monitoring and treat readiness as an operational proxy within a broader continuum of adaptation, maintenance, and maladaptation. [p. 2] - Monitoring tools should be “minimal, adequate, and accurate”: economical in burden, sufficient for a clearly defined decision, and supported by appropriate validity and reliability. [p. 3] - The framework separates what was done (training load), the athlete’s current condition (athlete state), and adaptation across longer time scales (training response), with interpretation depending on timing and context. [p. 8] - Individual reference values should be estimated from standardized repeated testing, with thresholds aligned to the timeframe and decision rather than calculated across periods that mix noise with true adaptation. [p. 15] - Distribution-based thresholds such as individual SD bands or minimum detectable change should be complemented by anchor-based practical importance and contextual information. [p. 15] - Threshold sensitivity should ref
LIM:  - Narrative source selection may omit conflicting evidence and cannot quantify the comparative validity or effectiveness of the proposed tools. - Direct experimental evidence that monitoring-informed training alone improves performance is limited. applied throughout to "Sport: American Football, Position: Wide Receiver" (p.2). Step One,
"Build Profile": a table of System, Notes, and Rationale covering Autonomic NS
(parasympathetic dominance, for "fast recovery abilities, resiliency"), Central NS (high
central drive, for "speed of movement, reaction time, tactical decision making"),
Neuromuscular (large fast-twitch percentage especially lower body, large concentric/eccentric
loading, for "speed of movement, deceleration qualities"), Energy Supply Systems (per
time-motion analysis: alactic and aerobic capacity), Common Injuries (ankle, knee, hip,
shoulder, fingers, informing "exercise prescription, loading strategies"), and
Anthropometrics (low body fat percent, moderate cross-sectional area for force production and
collisions). Step Two: "Setup Calendar" (competitions, travel, intensive practice periods,
organizational dates, holidays, training camps/facilities). Step Three: "Setup Periodization
Model" (single/double/triple periodization, team-sport considerations - the same
monocycle/bicycle/tricycle menu named in
[[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]], though this lecture does not say which one the
wide-receiver example uses). Step Four: "Setup Training Phases" (Preparatory-General/Specific,
Competition-Precompetitive/Main, Unloading/Tapering, Transition - see
[[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]]). Step Five: "Setup Bioenergetic Sequence"
(per athlete profile/TMA; aerobic, anaerobic-glycolytic, anaerobic-alactic; power vs.
capacity, time to develop, developmental potential). Step Six: "Setup Biodynamic Sequence"
(per profile, periodization model, phases, bioenergetics; exercises classified
GPE/SPE/SDE/Competitive - a classification already staged in this library's primary-source

speed, endurance, flexibility/mobility, skill; e.g. "Maximal-strength SPE vs SDE," "Alactic

"SLEEP ON IT" (p.13).

Heishman et al. 2020 — CMJ reliability with and without arm swing in Division I basketball
POP:  - Twenty-two NCAA Division I basketball players: 14 men and 8 women. - Participants were skilled jumpers from one intercollegiate program. - Reliability was assessed within sessions and across two sessions separated by at least one week. 
KEY:  - Most conventional CMJ variables and several alternative concentric/eccentric variables met both reliability criteria within and between sessions under both protocols. [p. 10] - Conventional measures such as concentric mean force, mean power, peak force, flight time, and jump height generally showed strong reliability, while flight-time-to-contraction-time ratio was less reliable with arm swing between sessions. [p. 5] - Several phase-duration and rate-of-force-development variables failed one or both reliability thresholds, with some coefficients of variation exceeding 20% and some ICCs below 0.70. [pp. 6-9] - The authors interpreted the no-arm-swing protocol as better suited to isolating lower-extremity function and acute readiness/fatigue, while arm swing may better represent longer-term changes in sport-specific jump performance. [p. 10] [p. 12] 
LIM:  - Training load during the testing period was not directly quantified; matching court time was used as an indirect control. [p. 12] - The cohort was small and relatively homogeneous, which can suppress between-athlete variability and reduce ICC estimates even when absolute repeatability is acceptab

Griffin et al. 2020 — ACWR evidence and application boundaries
POP:  - Participants: Athletes represented in 22 included articles. - Sport and level: Team-sport cohorts across the included literature. - Training or return-to-play context: Workload monitoring and non-contact injury occurrence. - Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Observational association literature
KEY:  - Twenty-two articles met the inclusion criteria; median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality was 8, with a range of 5 to 9. `[p. 1]` - The review reported associations between ACWR and non-contact injury but recommended its use only within a broader multifactorial monitoring system. `[p. 1]` - Both calculation models had support; the authors favored the exponentially weighted approach for sensitivity while noting that suitable windows and variables depend on the sport. `[p. 1]`
